blind.et: From Middle High German and Old High German blint, from Proto-West Germanic *blind.

s: A bolt of lightning lit the night.
Blitz.et:
From Middle High German blitze (“lightning”), from Old High German blëcchazzen; compare English bleak and bleach. Synchronically analyzed as a nominal formation from blitzen (“to flash”), see there for more.
Cognates
See also Old Saxon bliksmo (“lightning”), O…

Blitzkrieg.et: From Blitz (“lightning”) + Krieg (“war”), coined in the runup to the Second World War to denote the "lightning fast" military campaigns planned by the German forces.

s: arrester, lightning arrester, lightning conductor, lightning rod

Blick.et:
From Middle High German blic, from Old High German blik, from Proto-Germanic *blikaz, *blikkaz (“shine, appearance, look; metal”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleyǵ- (“to shine”).
Cognate with Dutch blik (“look, glance”), Danish blik (“look, glance; tin”), Icel…

s: a German surname with several clusters of use, the densest being in the Rhineland; spread to France and USA; most likely derived from a village and/or creek name Blissenbach in the Bergish Land
Originally the name of a German village, now merely an isolated street on a hill top outside the municipality of Kürten in the Bergish Land, east of Cologne.
Proper name of a brook or creek near Kürten in the Bergish Land east of Cologne in Germany.
to indicate (signal that one intends to turn left or right)
blinken.et: From Low German and Middle Low German blinken, ultimately from the root of blecken (“to bare”). Cognate with Dutch blinken.

s: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see blind, Passagier.

Blinddarm.et: blind (“blind”) + Darm (“intestine”), a partial calque of Latin caecum (“blind (thing)”).

s: to look (usually in a certain direction toward something)
blicken.et: From Middle High German blicken, from Old High German blicchen, from Proto-West Germanic *blik, from Proto-Germanic *bliką (“look”).

blitzen.et: From earlier blickzen, from Middle High German bleczen, from Old High German blechazan, bleckezzen, blekkezzen, from Proto-West Germanic *blikkattjan (“to shine, glitter”).

s: as quick as a flash, very fast

blindlings.et: Equivalent to blind + -lings. The formation is old; compare Old High German blintilingon.

blinzeln.et: From Middle High German blinzeln. Related to blinken (“to gleam, to twinkle”). Cognate with Luxembourgish blënzelen.

s: indicator (UK, Australia, New Zealand), turn signal (US), blinker (informal, US), direction indicator

Blitzeis.et: From Blitz (“lightning”) + Eis (“ice”). Coined in the early 1990s.

s: someone who fails to see or notice things
Blindschleiche.et: From Middle High German blintslīche, corresponding to blind + Schleicher, from schleichen (“to sneak; to slither”).

s: to erase someone's memories of a specific event
blitzdingsen.et: From the film Men In Black, called flashy-thing in the English original. The German calque is a compound of Blitz + Dings + -en.
